# DarkSlide v1.3.1

DarkSlide 1.3.1 adds flat-field calibration for RAW camera scans, improves decode and export performance, and fixes color clipping when converting Display P3 TIFF negatives. Processing stays local, and your original scans remain untouched.

## Highlights

- **Flat-field correction for RAW scans.** Correct lens vignetting and uneven illumination with a reference frame of the bare light source, captured with the same camera, lens, aperture, and light as your scans. Choose it in **Settings → Calibration**. Correction runs in linear light before film-base measurement, color balance, and starting exposure. The reference is normalized to the center, dust on the light source is ignored, and unsuitable references are refused. Scans from a different camera are left untouched and flagged.
- **Clipped film-base warning.** RAW imports now warn when clear film reaches the sensor limit in a channel. This helps you lower the capture exposure before clipping compromises the conversion.
- **Faster RAW imports.** The native decoder reuses its image parser for metadata, skips redundant work, and encodes pixels in parallel. On the tested 24 MP Nikon NEF, warm decode and binary packing dropped from roughly **530 ms to 255 ms**. Pixel preparation and calibration now run in the image worker, keeping the interface responsive.
- **Faster processing and steadier editing.** Rust WebAssembly accelerates high-depth conversion, geometry, and flat-field correction. Full-resolution color processing on the same scan was about **30% faster**, with identical results to the TypeScript reference. Tone edits reuse preview pixels and GPU uploads; dust repairs are reused until their marks or geometry change. Results depend on the scan and hardware.
- **Lower memory use and improved exports.** RAW recovery retains the file path and calibration snapshot instead of a second full-size pixel buffer. TIFF export processes bounded strips, 16-bit PNG uses compressed scanlines, and native folder saves pass binary bytes instead of large JSON arrays. Settings and batch dialogs load when first opened.

## TIFF color conversion

Display P3 color negatives are now inverted in their source color space before converting the positive into the requested output profile. Previously, converting the orange negative into the smaller sRGB gamut could clip channels before inversion and produce an artificial blue band.

Automatic film-base estimation also detects a reference that suppresses two color channels across most of the frame, even if the third channel hides the failure. It uses the existing conservative fallback; manually sampled film bases remain under your control.

These corrections can change the appearance of Display P3 TIFF conversions. White balance, exposure, and contrast may still need adjustment for the scan. Slides, LUT conversions, and the existing sRGB conversion order are preserved. RAW decoding uses Rawler 0.8, whose demosaicing fixes can produce small differences from earlier decoded images.

## Under the hood

Updated Rawler to 0.8, Tauri to 2.12 with matching plugins, React to 19.3, and Vite to 8.3. Rust kernels run inside the worker, with a TypeScript fallback when WebAssembly is unavailable. CI rebuilds and tests the kernels before packaging the desktop app.

See [performance measurements and reproduction instructions](https://github.com/kilianvivien/DarkSlide/blob/v1.3.1/PERFORMANCE.md) for the benchmark scope and implementation details.

## Desktop downloads

- **macOS:** universal Apple Silicon and Intel `.dmg`.
- **Windows:** `.msi` and NSIS `.exe` — experimental.
- **Linux:** `.deb` and `.AppImage` — experimental.

macOS builds are not notarized. On first launch, open the app through **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway** if required. Windows installers are unsigned. Windows and Linux builds are not yet production-tested.

## Validation

Type checking, ESLint, **923 JavaScript tests**, **12 native tests**, **2 Rust kernel tests**, and production builds passed locally. Validation included real NEF and Display P3 TIFF scans, an actual desktop RAW import, and a full-size **16-bit TIFF export with an embedded ICC profile**. TypeScript and Rust processing were compared on the same full-resolution input. The opt-in performance benchmark is skipped in the normal test suite.

## Credits

The flat-field approach follows [FreeCCR](https://github.com/toonoumi/FreeCCR) and [NegPy](https://github.com/marcinz606/NegPy), which correct uneven illumination in linear light before inversion. NegPy's scan-clip meter inspired the clipped-base warning. No code was copied from either project.
